response:
You should not keep paying for him. That needs to stop now.

Do not break up solely because he is poor before you first address the actual problem: you have been funding a relationship you cannot afford, volunteering to do it, and then suffering the consequences silently. The issue is not “he is poor,” it is “this relationship has developed spending habits that are damaging me.”

Tell him plainly, soon, and without hinting:

<message>I can't keep paying for your food, coffee, dates, or group expenses. I don't have the money. I've been overspending, using savings, and even lying to my parents about expenses, and that stops now. If we keep dating, we need to do things that cost little or nothing unless you already have your own budget for it.</message>

Also be specific about what changes:
<boundaries>
  <item>No more daily lunch or coffee spending for him.</item>
  <item>No more paying for both of you by default.</item>
  <item>No more expensive dates unless you can each afford your own share.</item>
  <item>No more covering social obligations like birthday dinners for the group.</item>
  <item>No more lying to your parents to patch over this.</item>
</boundaries>

Then change your behavior, not just your words. If you suggest a date, suggest things you can actually afford without paying for him:
<options>
  <item>walks</item>
  <item>campus time together</item>
  <item>free events</item>
  <item>tea or snacks only if each pays their own way</item>
  <item>staying in rather than movies or restaurants</item>
</options>

The key part: stop saying “it’s on me” unless you truly mean it and can comfortably afford it. Right now, your own choices are helping create the pattern you resent.

As for breaking up: don’t decide that before this conversation. Decide based on his response to a clear boundary.
<if>
  <case>If he understands, stops expecting money, and is willing to date within real limits, you may not need to break up.</case>
  <case>If he pressures you, guilt-trips you, keeps accepting money after you say no, or acts entitled to your allowance, then breaking up is reasonable.</case>
</if>

So the answer is:
<answer>
  <item>No, not immediately break up just because he is poor.</item>
  <item>Yes, immediately stop subsidizing him.</item>
  <item>Have one direct conversation and enforce the boundary.</item>
  <item>If the relationship cannot survive without your money, then it should end.</item>
</answer>

<steps>
  <step>Before the test, tell a teacher, school counselor, or accommodations office exactly what happens: “During exams I get so anxious I feel faint and can’t think straight.” That level of detail matters.</step>
  <step>Ask specifically about supports such as taking the test in a quieter room, short breaks, extra time, being seated near the door, or having a plan if you start to panic.</step>
  <step>Practice one simple calming routine ahead of time so it is familiar during the exam:
    <substep>Breathe in for 4, out for 6, for 1–2 minutes.</substep>
    <substep>Drop your shoulders and unclench your jaw and hands.</substep>
    <substep>Look around and name 5 things you see, 4 you feel, 3 you hear.</substep>
  </step>
  <step>During the test, do not fight the panic all at once. Focus on the next tiny action:
    <substep>Read one question.</substep>
    <substep>Underline key words.</substep>
    <substep>Answer the easiest question first.</substep>
    <substep>Move on and come back if your mind locks up.</substep>
  </step>
  <step>Use brief self-talk that is specific rather than dramatic: “This is anxiety, not danger. I only need to do the next step.”</step>

<advice>
    <point>
      Do not have a conversation whose hidden purpose is to get her to become comfortable with kissing or sex faster. That would almost certainly feel like pressure, even if you use gentle words.
    </point>
    <point>
      What you need to decide first, on your own, is this: can you genuinely be in a relationship with her at her current pace, with no expectation that it will change soon? If the honest answer is no, then the issue is compatibility, not persuasion.
    </point>
    <point>
      Do not tell her that her lack of kissing makes you feel like less of a man, hurts your self-esteem, or makes you question your attractiveness. Those are your feelings to process, but saying them to her in this context would load her boundary with guilt and make her feel responsible for reassuring you physically.
    </point>
    <point>
      Also do not bring up wanting sex before graduation. Given what she has already said and shown, that would be badly mismatched to her comfort level and would likely make her feel misunderstood or pressured.
    </point>
    <point>
      If you want to talk, make it a clarity-and-compatibility conversation, not a negotiation over her boundaries. A better approach would be something like:
      <example>
        "I want to talk honestly about where we are. I respect your boundaries, and I do not want you to do anything before you're ready. At the same time, I’m realizing I may want a relationship with a different level or pace of physical affection than what feels right to you. I’m not asking you to change for me. I just think we should be honest about whether we’re a good fit."
      </example>
    </point>
    <point>
      If she says she still is not ready and does not know when she will be, believe her. Do not interpret that as a challenge to overcome or as proof she secretly is not attracted to you. It may simply mean her comfort level, anxiety, orientation, or pace is different from yours.
    </point>
    <point>
      If you stay, stay without a countdown and without silently hoping patience will earn you sex or even a kiss by a certain date. If you cannot do that, ending the relationship is the more respectful option for both of you.
    </point>
    <point>
      In short: respect her boundary, stop tying your masculinity to whether she kisses you, and treat this as a compatibility decision. Either accept the relationship as it is, or end it kindly without making her feel at fault for not moving at your pace.
    </point>
  </advice>

response:
<advice>You should stop treating the central question as “What do these dreams mean?” and treat it as “What level of uncertainty requires transparency before we try for a baby?” On that question, the answer is clear: if this is enough to delay parenthood, it is enough to tell your husband about.</advice>
  <advice>Do not present it as “I have feelings for my ex,” because your post does not actually establish that. Present it more accurately: recurring dreams about an ex have stirred up unresolved feelings about that breakup, especially around apology and unfinished closure, and it is unexpectedly affecting your sense of readiness for a major life step. That is materially different from wanting to leave your marriage or reconnect with your ex.</advice>
  <advice>Tell your husband soon, and be specific. A useful version would be: “I need to explain why I pulled back. I’ve been having recurring dreams about my ex. I’m not hiding an affair, I don’t want him back, and this isn’t about loving you less. But the dreams have made me realize I may have some unresolved feelings about how that relationship ended, and I don’t want to start trying for a baby while I’m mentally unsettled and pretending everything is fine.”</advice>
  <advice>That conversation may make him uncomfortable, but discomfort is better than confusion. Right now he is being asked to accept a delay without being trusted with the reason. That is the part most likely to harm intimacy.</advice>
  <advice>With your therapist, stop accepting the “vivid imagination” line as the endpoint. Say directly: “When I bring this up and hear ‘vivid imagination,’ I feel dismissed. These dreams are affecting a major decision about starting a family, and I need help exploring whether this is unresolved grief, guilt, fear of transition, or something else.” If your therapist still will not engage with it seriously, consider a few sessions with someone else specifically for this issue.</advice>
  <advice>Also, do not over-literalize dreams. The content you describe could point to unfinished grief, guilt about how the breakup happened, anxiety about irreversible adulthood milestones, or your mind revisiting a period when one life path closed and another began. Starting a family often stirs old identity material. None of that requires that your ex is your true desire or that your marriage is wrong.</advice>
  <advice>Do not contact the ex for “closure” unless you have done substantial work first and have a very clear therapeutic reason. In situations like this, people often imagine that one conversation will cleanly resolve the feeling, but it can just as easily intensify it, disrupt your marriage, and confuse what is currently an internal process.</advice>
  <advice>For now, set a short, concrete pause rather than an indefinite delay: talk to your husband, revisit this in therapy with more force, journal the recurring themes in the dreams, and reassess after a defined period. That keeps this from turning into a vague cloud with outsized power.</advice>
  <advice>The important correction is this: you do not need to solve the ex before you can be a good partner or future parent, but you do need to be honest that something unresolved has been activated and that it is affecting your readiness. That honesty is the next responsible step.</advice>

    <point>Do these in the next 24 hours:</point>
    <steps>
      <step>Email your academic advisor and campus counselor today. Keep it short: say your mental health is seriously interfering with attendance, tests, and homework, and you need urgent help making a plan to stay afloat this term.</step>
      <step>Email each professor today or tomorrow, even if you are embarrassed. Say you have been dealing with significant mental-health difficulties that are affecting attendance and coursework, you are contacting campus support, and you want to know the fastest way to minimize further damage in the course.</step>
      <step>Ask one concrete question in each email: “What should I prioritize first?” This makes it easier for them to give you an actionable answer instead of a vague response.</step>
    </steps>
    <point>Stop trying to mentally solve the whole semester. Only solve the next appearance. Your target can be as small as:</point>
    <steps>
      <step>get out of bed</step>
      <step>put on clothes</step>
      <step>walk to the building</step>
      <step>sit in class for 10 minutes</step>
      <step>if you cannot stay, leave after those 10 minutes and count it as a partial win</step>
    </steps>
    <point>This works because avoidance shrinks when you repeatedly face the situation in small doses. The goal at first is attendance, not perfect performance.</point>
    <point>For tests and assignments, use triage, not idealism:</point>
    <steps>
      <step>List every class.</step>
      <step>For each one, identify the next graded item or the easiest missing item worth points.</step>
      <step>Do the highest-impact, lowest-effort task first.</step>
      <step>Ignore catching up “correctly.” Right now, preserving points matters more than doing everything in order.</step>
    </steps>
    <point>If a class feels impossible to enter, reduce the barrier further: arrive early and sit near the door, ask a friend to walk with you, or tell yourself you only have to stay until attendance is taken or until the break.</point>
    <point>Also make a decision rule for the week: unless you are physically unable, you go to class without debating it. Anxiety gets stronger when it is allowed to negotiate with you every morning.</point>
    <point>When you meet the counselor, ask specifically about emergency academic options, not just emotional support: temporary accommodations, reduced course load, incompletes, extensions, medical documentation, or withdrawal deadlines. You do not need to decide on a full break today, but you do need to know your options now.</point>
    <point>If your anxiety becomes so intense that you feel unsafe, hopeless, or at risk of harming yourself, treat that as an urgent situation and contact emergency mental-health support, a crisis line, or campus emergency services immediately.</point>
    <point>A simple script you can send to professors:</point>
    <example>Hello Professor, I have been dealing with significant mental-health difficulties that have affected my attendance and ability to complete work. I am contacting campus counseling/advising for support now. I know I have fallen behind, and I want to minimize further damage in your course. Can you tell me what I should prioritize first and whether there are any immediate steps I should take? Thank you.</example>

response:
<advice>You were not wrong to report repeated theft of food you paid for and intended for students. The key moral point is simple: you reported an ongoing problem through a supervisor after trying less confrontational options. Someone else chose surveillance, and management chose termination. The custodian lost his job because he stole, not because you mentioned missing snacks.</advice>
  <advice>That said, your immediate problem now is not whether you were justified; it is the hostility at work. Treat that as a separate issue and respond to it directly. Stop trying to relitigate the theft with coworkers. Use a short, consistent line: “I reported repeated theft of supplies I bought for students after trying to handle it quietly. I was not involved in the decision to use a camera or terminate anyone.” Then disengage.</advice>
  <advice>Document the retaliation or hostility in a factual log: date, person, what was said or done, and any witnesses. If the treatment is affecting your work, bring that documentation to your principal or HR and frame it as a professional climate problem, not a gossip dispute.</advice>
  <advice>Do not quit quickly over this unless you already intended to leave for broader reasons. As a first-year teacher, a hostile patch can feel total, but a midyear resignation may hurt you professionally and will likely hurt students more than staying while you seek support.</advice>
  <advice>Also, stop personally absorbing this need by yourself if you can. Ask administration, counseling, social work, the PTA, or a community partner whether there is a formal snack pantry, approved donation process, or student-support fund. If you continue keeping food, get clarity on school policy about storage and allergens so you are not carrying avoidable risk alone.</advice>

<response>
  <advice>You were not wrong to report repeated theft of food you paid for and intended for students. The key moral point is simple: you reported an ongoing problem through a supervisor after trying less confrontational options. Someone else chose surveillance, and management chose termination. The custodian lost his job because he stole, not because you mentioned missing snacks.</advice>
  <advice>That said, your immediate problem now is not whether you were justified; it is the hostility at work. Treat that as a separate issue and respond to it directly. Stop trying to relitigate the theft with coworkers. Use a short, consistent line: “I reported repeated theft of supplies I bought for students after trying to handle it quietly. I was not involved in the decision to use a camera or terminate anyone.” Then disengage.</advice>
  <advice>Document the retaliation or hostility in a factual log: date, person, what was said or done, and any witnesses. If the treatment is affecting your work, bring that documentation to your principal or HR and frame it as a professional climate problem, not a gossip dispute.</advice>
  <advice>Do not quit quickly over this unless you already intended to leave for broader reasons. As a first-year teacher, a hostile patch can feel total, but a midyear resignation may hurt you professionally and will likely hurt students more than staying while you seek support.</advice>
  <advice>Also, stop personally absorbing this need by yourself if you can. Ask administration, counseling, social work, the PTA, or a community partner whether there is a formal snack pantry, approved donation process, or student-support fund. If you continue keeping food, get clarity on school policy about storage and allergens so you are not carrying avoidable risk alone.</advice>
  <advice>If you want to repair relationships, do it selectively and without apologizing for reporting theft. You can say: “I regret how this escalated, but I couldn’t keep replacing food bought for students.” That acknowledges the disruption without accepting blame for someone else’s misconduct.</advice>
  <advice>The practical next steps are: document the hostility, give one neutral explanation when necessary, escalate workplace retaliation through proper channels, and look for institutional support for student snacks. Those are better moves than resigning in reaction to gossip.</advice>
</response>

    <point>
      Do not resign until you have a written offer, compensation details, start date, and clarity on whether the new company requires a current-manager reference or only an employment verification.
    </point>
    <point>
      Address the reference issue directly and professionally now, before your current boss is contacted. Say something like: “My current manager is aware I handle a broad mix of duties, but our working relationship is strained and I’m concerned he may not provide an objective performance reference. I’m happy to provide prior managers, coworkers, clients, or other references, and you may verify my current employment through HR/payroll instead.” This is transparent without sounding vindictive.
    </point>
    <point>
      If they insist on speaking with your current employer, ask whether they can limit it to employment verification only: dates, title, and eligibility for rehire if applicable. Many companies will accommodate this, especially for candidates who are still employed.
    </point>
    <point>
      Gather backup evidence now: previous supervisors, older referrals, written praise, performance metrics, campaign results, examples of content, screenshots of positive outcomes, and anything showing that you handled patient inquiries, scheduling, and marketing work effectively. If your current boss is unreliable, objective evidence matters.
    </point>
    <point>
      Do not tell your boss you are leaving until the new employer has finished any checks that could be affected by him. Given the specific risk you described, early disclosure serves you poorly.
    </point>
    <point>
      Once the new job is confirmed, resign briefly and professionally. Keep the message simple: your last day, appreciation for the opportunity, and willingness to hand off key items during the notice period. Do not argue about his treatment, and do not try to win his agreement about why you are leaving.
    </point>
    <point>
      If you can safely give notice, do so and use that time to create a short transition document: pending leads, ad accounts, passwords access process if appropriate, scheduled content, patient inquiry status, open vendors, and recurring tasks. That protects coworkers and strengthens your professionalism.
    </point>
    <point>
      But if there is a real risk of retaliation, verbal abuse, sabotage of the new job, or being fired immediately after notice, it is ethically acceptable to reduce notice or leave immediately once your new role is secure. Your obligation is to act professionally, not to expose yourself to harm.
    </point>
    <point>
      Do not confront him by accusing him of abuse in the resignation conversation unless you are prepared for escalation and have a concrete purpose. In most cases, the cleanest exit is the best exit.
    </point>
    <point>
      For the new company, frame your reason for leaving around fit and scope: “I’m seeking a role focused on marketing where I can work with more autonomy and clearer priorities.” That is honest and avoids sounding dramatic.
    </point>
    <point>
      If your current boss does give a hostile reference and the offer is threatened, respond once, calmly, with facts: your actual duties, examples of results, and alternative references. Do not launch into a long personal complaint. Hiring managers usually recognize when one manager is unusually negative.
    </point>

<response>
  <advice>
    <point>
      Do not resign until you have a written offer, compensation details, start date, and clarity on whether the new company requires a current-manager reference or only an employment verification.
    </point>
    <point>
      Address the reference issue directly and professionally now, before your current boss is contacted. Say something like: “My current manager is aware I handle a broad mix of duties, but our working relationship is strained and I’m concerned he may not provide an objective performance reference. I’m happy to provide prior managers, coworkers, clients, or other references, and you may verify my current employment through HR/payroll instead.” This is transparent without sounding vindictive.
    </point>
    <point>
      If they insist on speaking with your current employer, ask whether they can limit it to employment verification only: dates, title, and eligibility for rehire if applicable. Many companies will accommodate this, especially for candidates who are still employed.
    </point>
    <point>
      Gather backup evidence now: previous supervisors, older referrals, written praise, performance metrics, campaign results, examples of content, screenshots of positive outcomes, and anything showing that you handled patient inquiries, scheduling, and marketing work effectively. If your current boss is unreliable, objective evidence matters.
    </point>
    <point>
      Do not tell your boss you are leaving until the new employer has finished any checks that could be affected by him. Given the specific risk you described, early disclosure serves you poorly.
    </point>
    <point>
      Once the new job is confirmed, resign briefly and professionally. Keep the message simple: your last day, appreciation for the opportunity, and willingness to hand off key items during the notice period. Do not argue about his treatment, and do not try to win his agreement about why you are leaving.
    </point>
    <point>
      If you can safely give notice, do so and use that time to create a short transition document: pending leads, ad accounts, passwords access process if appropriate, scheduled content, patient inquiry status, open vendors, and recurring tasks. That protects coworkers and strengthens your professionalism.
    </point>
    <point>
      But if there is a real risk of retaliation, verbal abuse, sabotage of the new job, or being fired immediately after notice, it is ethically acceptable to reduce notice or leave immediately once your new role is secure. Your obligation is to act professionally, not to expose yourself to harm.
    </point>
    <point>
      Do not confront him by accusing him of abuse in the resignation conversation unless you are prepared for escalation and have a concrete purpose. In most cases, the cleanest exit is the best exit.
    </point>
    <point>
      For the new company, frame your reason for leaving around fit and scope: “I’m seeking a role focused on marketing where I can work with more autonomy and clearer priorities.” That is honest and avoids sounding dramatic.
    </point>
    <point>
      If your current boss does give a hostile reference and the offer is threatened, respond once, calmly, with facts: your actual duties, examples of results, and alternative references. Do not launch into a long personal complaint. Hiring managers usually recognize when one manager is unusually negative.
    </point>
  </advice>
  <script>
    <to_new_employer>
      “I want to be transparent about references. I’m currently employed, and my manager may not be the best source for an objective performance reference due to a strained working relationship. I’d be glad to provide previous supervisors and other professional references, and you’re welcome to verify my current employment through official channels.”
    </to_new_employer>
    <resignation_note>
      “Please accept this as my notice of resignation. My last working day will be [date]. Thank you for the opportunity. I will do my best to hand over active marketing, scheduling, and administrative items before I leave.”
    </resignation_note>
  </script>
  <bottomline>
    Your best path is: secure the offer first, proactively manage the reference issue with the new employer, then resign briefly and professionally with whatever notice is realistically safe. Do not give your current boss an early chance to interfere with the new job.
  </bottomline>
</response>

response:
<advice>
    <point>
      Stop using bleach for this job. It is not helping much with label removal, and it adds avoidable issues: fumes, residue, possible plastic damage, and extra rinsing before disposal or recycling.
    </point>
    <point>
      Use a simpler process: empty the bottles fully, rinse them, then soak them in warm or hot soapy water. Many prescription labels will loosen after that. For adhesive left behind, use a little cooking oil, rubbing alcohol, or a commercial adhesive remover on the label area, then wash again.
    </point>
    <point>
      If the labels still do not come off easily, a faster privacy method is to physically destroy the labeled section rather than trying to make the whole bottle pristine. Cut or shred the part of the bottle containing your name, prescription number, doctor, and pharmacy details. Dispose of those label fragments in a separate trash bag from the bottles if you want extra protection.
    </point>
    <point>
      If you have many bottles, process them in small batches so they do not take over shared space. Keep the work area ventilated and dry the bottles before placing them in recycling or trash.
    </point>
    <point>
      Check your local recycling rules before putting the bottles in curbside recycling. Some areas accept these plastics only if they are clean and empty; others do not. If your pharmacy has a take-back or bottle-recycling program, that may be easier.
    </point>
    <point>
      Also make sure there is no medication left inside. Leftover medicine should be disposed of through a pharmacy or community drug take-back program, not left in the bottles.
    </point>
    <point>
      A practical routine is: remove or destroy the label, rinse the bottle, confirm local recycling rules, then recycle or trash accordingly. That addresses the real privacy issue more effectively than prolonged bleach soaking.
    </point>
  </advice>

<response>
  <advice>
    <point>
      Stop using bleach for this job. It is not helping much with label removal, and it adds avoidable issues: fumes, residue, possible plastic damage, and extra rinsing before disposal or recycling.
    </point>
    <point>
      Use a simpler process: empty the bottles fully, rinse them, then soak them in warm or hot soapy water. Many prescription labels will loosen after that. For adhesive left behind, use a little cooking oil, rubbing alcohol, or a commercial adhesive remover on the label area, then wash again.
    </point>
    <point>
      If the labels still do not come off easily, a faster privacy method is to physically destroy the labeled section rather than trying to make the whole bottle pristine. Cut or shred the part of the bottle containing your name, prescription number, doctor, and pharmacy details. Dispose of those label fragments in a separate trash bag from the bottles if you want extra protection.
    </point>
    <point>
      If you have many bottles, process them in small batches so they do not take over shared space. Keep the work area ventilated and dry the bottles before placing them in recycling or trash.
    </point>
    <point>
      Check your local recycling rules before putting the bottles in curbside recycling. Some areas accept these plastics only if they are clean and empty; others do not. If your pharmacy has a take-back or bottle-recycling program, that may be easier.
    </point>
    <point>
      Also make sure there is no medication left inside. Leftover medicine should be disposed of through a pharmacy or community drug take-back program, not left in the bottles.
    </point>
    <point>
      A practical routine is: remove or destroy the label, rinse the bottle, confirm local recycling rules, then recycle or trash accordingly. That addresses the real privacy issue more effectively than prolonged bleach soaking.
    </point>
  </advice>
</response>

response:
<advice>
    <point>Act as if the relationship is over. His behavior already communicated that, even though he handled it badly and indirectly.</point>
    <point>Do not contact him again, and do not contact his friends, coworkers, or family for more answers. There is very little chance of getting satisfying closure from someone who chose avoidance and blocking.</point>
    <point>Remove the sources that keep reopening the wound: stop checking his Instagram, mute/block him if needed, delete the chat from easy view, and ask mutual contacts not to update you about him.</point>
    <point>Your immediate problem is not figuring him out; it is stabilizing your body and mind. For sleep tonight, do something structured: put your phone away for an hour before bed, take a shower, drink water, write down the facts of what happened on paper, and use a simple repeating thought like “I do not need more answers tonight.”</point>

response:
Tell your boyfriend, clearly and immediately, that this arrangement ends now. Not “soon,” not “when it feels less awkward,” and not as a discussion about curtains or slippers.

What matters most is this: you are displaced from your own bed, losing privacy while working, and living with an open-ended guest your boyfriend refuses to manage. That is no longer a minor hosting inconvenience. It is a household failure, and your boyfriend is participating in it.

Do this in concrete steps:

1. Stop treating this as a list of annoyances.
The issue is not really burping, TV, or meal timing. The issue is:
- the guest was invited for 1–2 weeks and has stayed over a month,
- there is no firm departure date,
- your boyfriend refuses to enforce one,
- you have lost access to your own bedroom and normal use of your home.

Frame it that way.

2. Give your boyfriend one direct statement.
Say something like:

“Your friend was supposed to stay 1–2 weeks. It has been over a month. I am no longer willing to live like this, and I am not giving up my bed or my privacy anymore. He needs to leave by [specific date, very soon]. I need you to tell him today.”

Do not argue the details point by point. Stay on the deadline and the living arrangement.

3. If your boyfriend refuses, speak to the friend yourself.
Because your boyfriend is not handling his guest, you may need to. Keep it short and factual:

“When we agreed to this, it was for 1–2 weeks. It has now been over a month, and this arrangement is no longer working. You need to make other arrangements and move out by [date].”

You do not need to justify this with a long complaint list. The original agreement already justifies it.

4. Reclaim your room immediately.
Tonight, not later.
If the master bedroom is your shared bedroom, you sleep there. The guest sleeps in the study/daybed or leaves. The current setup is unacceptable.

Your wake-up time is not a reason for you to be exiled from your own bed. Adults hosting guests do not surrender the primary bedroom indefinitely.

5. Set house rules out loud, not by adaptation.
For the remaining time he is there:
- Your work room is off-limits during work hours.
- He does not use your slippers.
- You and your boyfriend eat on your own schedule.
- You choose TV sometimes, or use the living room without him.
- Curtains stay open where the plants need light.

State these directly. Do not keep silently adjusting.

6. Check the lease if needed.
If your boyfriend still will not act and the guest still will not leave, review the lease’s guest policy. A month-plus stay may already be a problem. You do not have to threaten this first, but you should know your position.

7. Pay attention to what your boyfriend is showing you.
The biggest problem may not be the guest. It may be that your boyfriend is comfortable letting you be displaced, uncomfortable, and ignored in your own home to avoid an awkward conversation with his friend.

That deserves serious attention. Even if the friend leaves tomorrow, you still need to address this with him:
- Why did he laugh it off?
- Why is his friend’s comfort taking priority over yours?
- Why are you the one sleeping in the study and crying alone while he does nothing?

If he cannot or will not answer that well, treat that as relationship information.

So the immediate advice is simple:
set a move-out date, reclaim your bed, stop accommodating, and if your boyfriend won’t manage his guest, do it yourself.

<response>
Tell your boyfriend, clearly and immediately, that this arrangement ends now. Not “soon,” not “when it feels less awkward,” and not as a discussion about curtains or slippers.

What matters most is this: you are displaced from your own bed, losing privacy while working, and living with an open-ended guest your boyfriend refuses to manage. That is no longer a minor hosting inconvenience. It is a household failure, and your boyfriend is participating in it.

Do this in concrete steps:

1. Stop treating this as a list of annoyances.
The issue is not really burping, TV, or meal timing. The issue is:
- the guest was invited for 1–2 weeks and has stayed over a month,
- there is no firm departure date,
- your boyfriend refuses to enforce one,
- you have lost access to your own bedroom and normal use of your home.

Frame it that way.

2. Give your boyfriend one direct statement.
Say something like:

“Your friend was supposed to stay 1–2 weeks. It has been over a month. I am no longer willing to live like this, and I am not giving up my bed or my privacy anymore. He needs to leave by [specific date, very soon]. I need you to tell him today.”

Do not argue the details point by point. Stay on the deadline and the living arrangement.

3. If your boyfriend refuses, speak to the friend yourself.
Because your boyfriend is not handling his guest, you may need to. Keep it short and factual:

“When we agreed to this, it was for 1–2 weeks. It has now been over a month, and this arrangement is no longer working. You need to make other arrangements and move out by [date].”

You do not need to justify this with a long complaint list. The original agreement already justifies it.

4. Reclaim your room immediately.
Tonight, not later.
If the master bedroom is your shared bedroom, you sleep there. The guest sleeps in the study/daybed or leaves. The current setup is unacceptable.

Your wake-up time is not a reason for you to be exiled from your own bed. Adults hosting guests do not surrender the primary bedroom indefinitely.

5. Set house rules out loud, not by adaptation.
For the remaining time he is there:
- Your work room is off-limits during work hours.
- He does not use your slippers.
- You and your boyfriend eat on your own schedule.
- You choose TV sometimes, or use the living room without him.
- Curtains stay open where the plants need light.

State these directly. Do not keep silently adjusting.

6. Check the lease if needed.
If your boyfriend still will not act and the guest still will not leave, review the lease’s guest policy. A month-plus stay may already be a problem. You do not have to threaten this first, but you should know your position.

7. Pay attention to what your boyfriend is showing you.
The biggest problem may not be the guest. It may be that your boyfriend is comfortable letting you be displaced, uncomfortable, and ignored in your own home to avoid an awkward conversation with his friend.

That deserves serious attention. Even if the friend leaves tomorrow, you still need to address this with him:
- Why did he laugh it off?
- Why is his friend’s comfort taking priority over yours?
- Why are you the one sleeping in the study and crying alone while he does nothing?

If he cannot or will not answer that well, treat that as relationship information.

So the immediate advice is simple:
set a move-out date, reclaim your bed, stop accommodating, and if your boyfriend won’t manage his guest, do it yourself.</response>

<advice>
    <point>You need to treat this as both an anxiety problem and a safety problem. Because you’re having suicidal thoughts and sometimes can’t make yourself eat or drink, the first priority is getting more support than “just trying harder” on your own.</point>

    <point>If you might act on suicidal thoughts, if you feel unable to stay safe, or if you’re going without food or fluids to the point you may be medically at risk, contact emergency services now or go to the nearest emergency department. If you can, tell someone in your home or a trusted person immediately and do not stay alone with it.</point>

    <point>If you are not in immediate danger but the thoughts are recurring, contact a crisis line today and make a same-day safety plan with a real person. If you’re in the U.S. or Canada, call or text 988. If you’re elsewhere, contact your local crisis service or emergency number. Tell them plainly: “I’m having suicidal thoughts, severe anxiety, and I’m struggling to eat and drink.”</point>

    <point>You also need a higher level or different type of care than what you’ve had before. Since multiple therapists have not helped enough, ask specifically for one of these:
      <subpoint>a psychiatrist for medication evaluation if you do not already have one,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>an intensive outpatient program (IOP) or partial hospitalization program (PHP),</subpoint>
      <subpoint>a therapist who specializes in anxiety disorders/OCD and exposure-based treatment,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>assessment for agoraphobia, social anxiety, trauma-related symptoms, panic disorder, avoidant patterns, and eating/self-neglect risk.</subpoint>
    </point>

    <point>When you contact providers, don’t just say “anxiety.” Say exactly what is happening: “I’m mostly housebound, I panic when I go out, I dropped out of school because of breakdowns, I’ve had suicidal thoughts since childhood, and I sometimes lack the will to eat or drink.” That wording makes the severity clearer.</point>

    <point>Stop making “leave the house normally and perform well” the goal for now. Your current target should be tiny, repeatable exposures that do not end in total exhaustion. For example:
      <subpoint>stand at the door for 30 seconds,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>step outside for 1 minute,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>walk to the end of the path or building entrance,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>repeat the same step daily until it feels a little less intense.</subpoint>
      The point is not bravery in one big burst; it’s retraining your nervous system through small repetition.</point>

    <point>Before exposures, make a short script so you don’t have to think under stress: “My job is only to stand outside for one minute. I do not need to look normal. I do not need to talk well. I only need to complete the minute.”</point>

    <point>For panic, use simple grounding rather than arguing with the panic:
      <subpoint>lengthen the exhale: inhale 4, exhale 6, for a few rounds,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>name 5 things you see, 4 you feel, 3 you hear,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>drop your shoulders and unclench your jaw,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>carry water or something cold to hold.</subpoint>
      These won’t erase anxiety, but they can reduce the spike enough to stay in the situation a little longer.</point>

    <point>Because eating and drinking are slipping, set “minimum survival tasks” for each day. Make the bar very low and specific:
      <subpoint>drink one glass of water within 30 minutes of waking,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>eat one easy food even if it’s small,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>take a shower or wash face,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>step outside or open the door,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>message one person or one service.</subpoint>
      Do not wait for willpower. Use alarms, notes, or ask someone to prompt you.</point>

    <point>If there is any trusted person at all—family member, old friend, neighbor—tell them directly: “I’m not doing well mentally, I’m having suicidal thoughts, and I need help making appointments and getting out of the house.” Do not make them guess.</point>

    <point>It may help to separate two beliefs that are currently fused together: “I feel incapable” and “I am incapable.” The first is a symptom state. The second is a conclusion. Your actions already show they are not identical: you’ve kept trying to go out, kept seeking treatment, and you still want a life. That means the system is jammed, not gone.</point>

    <point>For the next 24 hours, make the plan concrete:
      <subpoint>1. Remove or create distance from anything you could use to harm yourself if possible.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>2. Contact a crisis line or emergency support if safety is shaky.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>3. Book one urgent appointment with a doctor, psychiatrist, or clinic and use the exact severity details.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>4. Drink water and eat something easy.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>5. Do one tiny outside exposure only, not a major outing.</subpoint>
    </point>

    <point>If you want, I can help you make a one-page crisis/safety plan or draft a message to a doctor or therapist that explains your situation clearly.</point>
  </advice>

response:
<advice>You should not cancel the trip, and you should not involve your parents right now unless the messages become abusive, threatening, or nonstop.</advice>
  <advice>Your actual mistake was the delivery, not the decision. You gave very short notice and let the news travel through your parents. That likely made an old wound worse. Own that part plainly without apologizing for taking the trip.</advice>
  <advice>Send one direct message to your siblings yourself. Keep it short, firm, and non-defensive. Something like: “I should have told you all directly, and earlier. I understand that hearing this last-minute from Mom and Dad may have felt hurtful. But this trip is about supporting my in-laws after Gabriel’s death, and I’m not going to debate that choice. I’m happy to talk after the holidays if we can do it respectfully.”</advice>
  <advice>Do not argue point-by-point with the texts. If you start defending your entire history with the family, you will get pulled into a much older fight that cannot be solved over Christmas messages.</advice>
  <advice>If any sibling keeps attacking you, repeat the boundary once: “I’m not continuing this conversation if you insult me.” After that, mute or stop responding. You do not need to absorb punishment to prove you care.</advice>
  <advice>Do not show your parents the messages just to get backup. That would turn this into a parents-versus-siblings conflict. Only bring them in if there is harassment, threats, or behavior serious enough that silence would be irresponsible.</advice>
  <advice>After the holiday, decide whether you want a real conversation with your siblings about the deeper issue. If you do, keep it focused: they may feel long-term distance from you, but they do not get to weaponize your grief or your care for your in-laws. Both things can be true at once: they may have unresolved hurt, and they were still wrong to unload on you like this.</advice>
  <advice>For the future, communicate directly and earlier, especially around holidays. That will not erase the underlying family tension, but it will remove the easy target of “you blindsided us.”</advice>

response:
<advice>
    <point>Do not move in unless this is resolved first. On the facts you gave, yes, you would very likely become miserable and resentful if you moved in now.</point>
    <point>Stop cleaning his house to this extent. You are not getting useful information anymore; you already have it. The current pattern lets him continue as he is while you absorb the discomfort and labor.</point>
    <point>Have one direct conversation, not hints, not excuses. Say plainly: “I am not willing to move into a house kept at this standard. This is not about perfection or OCD. I need a home that is basically clean, hygienic, and safe. Right now the mess, dirty surfaces, toilets, and clutter on the floor make me not want to live there.”</point>
    <point>Be specific about behaviors, not global character judgments. Mention concrete examples: rubbish and letters on the floor, screws and wires creating hazards, dirty kitchen surfaces, unclean toilets, dirty floors, and the fact that cleaning done by you is not maintained.</point>
    <point>Do not argue about whether you are “OCD.” That label is a distraction. Bring it back to minimum living standards and division of labor.</point>
    <point>Set a clear condition for cohabitation: “I will only consider moving in if you can consistently maintain the house at a basic standard on your own first.” That means before you move in, not after.</point>
    <point>Ask for a trial period of demonstrated change, not promises. For example: for the next 6–8 weeks, he keeps floors clear, kitchen counters wiped, dishes dealt with daily, toilets cleaned weekly, rubbish and recycling managed, and no hazardous clutter left around. You do not manage this for him.</point>
    <point>If he says he works a lot or that he does not care, the answer is not that you should take over. The answer is that you may be incompatible for living together unless he hires help or changes his habits.</point>
    <point>If he genuinely wants you there and wants your financial contribution, then household standards and labor must be discussed as seriously as rent or mortgage contributions. You should not pay to become the live-in cleaner.</point>
    <point>Do not soften this by inventing reasons to delay. Tell him the truth kindly and directly. Something like: “I love being with you, but I am avoiding moving in because I do not want to live in the house as it is currently kept.”</point>
    <point>Then watch his response carefully. The important test is not whether he says thank you or says you do not have to clean. The test is whether he accepts the issue as real, takes responsibility, and changes his behavior consistently without you managing him.</point>
    <point>If he minimizes it, calls you controlling, insists this is just your problem, or waits for you to resume cleaning, treat that as your answer. You can keep the relationship and not move in, but you should not enter cohabitation expecting him to become different once you are there.</point>
  </advice>

<response>
  <advice>
    <point>Do not move in unless this is resolved first. On the facts you gave, yes, you would very likely become miserable and resentful if you moved in now.</point>
    <point>Stop cleaning his house to this extent. You are not getting useful information anymore; you already have it. The current pattern lets him continue as he is while you absorb the discomfort and labor.</point>
    <point>Have one direct conversation, not hints, not excuses. Say plainly: “I am not willing to move into a house kept at this standard. This is not about perfection or OCD. I need a home that is basically clean, hygienic, and safe. Right now the mess, dirty surfaces, toilets, and clutter on the floor make me not want to live there.”</point>
    <point>Be specific about behaviors, not global character judgments. Mention concrete examples: rubbish and letters on the floor, screws and wires creating hazards, dirty kitchen surfaces, unclean toilets, dirty floors, and the fact that cleaning done by you is not maintained.</point>
    <point>Do not argue about whether you are “OCD.” That label is a distraction. Bring it back to minimum living standards and division of labor.</point>
    <point>Set a clear condition for cohabitation: “I will only consider moving in if you can consistently maintain the house at a basic standard on your own first.” That means before you move in, not after.</point>
    <point>Ask for a trial period of demonstrated change, not promises. For example: for the next 6–8 weeks, he keeps floors clear, kitchen counters wiped, dishes dealt with daily, toilets cleaned weekly, rubbish and recycling managed, and no hazardous clutter left around. You do not manage this for him.</point>
    <point>If he says he works a lot or that he does not care, the answer is not that you should take over. The answer is that you may be incompatible for living together unless he hires help or changes his habits.</point>
    <point>If he genuinely wants you there and wants your financial contribution, then household standards and labor must be discussed as seriously as rent or mortgage contributions. You should not pay to become the live-in cleaner.</point>
    <point>Do not soften this by inventing reasons to delay. Tell him the truth kindly and directly. Something like: “I love being with you, but I am avoiding moving in because I do not want to live in the house as it is currently kept.”</point>
    <point>Then watch his response carefully. The important test is not whether he says thank you or says you do not have to clean. The test is whether he accepts the issue as real, takes responsibility, and changes his behavior consistently without you managing him.</point>
    <point>If he minimizes it, calls you controlling, insists this is just your problem, or waits for you to resume cleaning, treat that as your answer. You can keep the relationship and not move in, but you should not enter cohabitation expecting him to become different once you are there.</point>
  </advice>

      Start by gathering everything:
      <items>

        <item>the wedding date, timeline, and no-show details</item>
        <item>any costs caused by the no-show</item>
      </items>
    </point>
    <point>
      Send one calm written demand. Keep it brief and factual:
      <items>
        <item>state that she did not appear and gave no notice</item>
        <item>state what remedy you want</item>
        <item>set a clear deadline for response</item>
        <item>say that if unresolved, you will pursue the next formal options available</item>
      </items>
    </point>
    <point>
      If she does not respond, consider proportionate escalation:
      <items>
        <item>payment dispute if applicable</item>
        <item>small claims court if the amount justifies it</item>
        <item>a complaint to any relevant licensing or business body if one applies</item>
        <item>a truthful public review limited to verifiable facts</item>
      </items>
    </point>
    <point>
      If you leave a review, make it read like evidence, not anger. Include only specifics you can back up: booked date, payment made, she did not attend, no notice given, response afterward. Avoid insults, threats, or speculation about intent unless you can prove it.

    <point>
      Talk with your spouse before you do anything public. Make sure the plan is about protecting your interests and warning others fairly, not venting.
    </point>
    <point>
      The strongest position is: factual, documented, and proportionate. That is much more likely to produce consequences she will actually feel than revenge-driven actions.
    </point>
  </advice>

    <step>First, find out whether you can still withdraw from the class, take a late withdrawal, or if you are definitely headed for a failing grade. Check the syllabus, then contact your professor and your academic advisor immediately. Ask one direct question: “Given my current grades, is there any realistic path to passing, or should I withdraw if that is still possible?”</step>
    <step>If withdrawal is still possible and passing is realistically out of reach, strongly consider withdrawing instead of taking the F. Your advisor can tell you how a W versus an F affects your transcript, GPA, and academic standing at your college.</step>

response:
<advice>
    <point>
      Treat this as a self-image adjustment problem, not proof that your progress "doesn't count." Your body changed faster than your internal picture of yourself did. That lag is common.
    </point>
    <point>
      Stop using the old label "heavy and unattractive person" as if it were your identity. You used to have a different body size; that is not the same thing as being permanently unattractive or flawed. Each time that thought shows up, replace it with something factual: "My body has changed, my habits have changed, and my self-image is catching up."
    </point>
    <point>
      Use objective anchors instead of relying on your mood in the mirror. Keep track of a few concrete markers: how your clothes fit, progress photos taken at set intervals, workout performance, labs or health markers if you have them, and energy levels. When your brain says "nothing is different," compare that thought to evidence.
    </point>
    <point>
      Limit body-checking and harsh mirror analysis. Looking repeatedly for flaws tends to strengthen the old mental image. When you do look, keep it brief and neutral: notice posture, fit, and changes without turning it into a judgment session.
    </point>
    <point>
      Work on body neutrality before body confidence. You do not need to force yourself to feel attractive every day. A more realistic goal is: "This is my body. It is stronger and healthier than before. I can take care of it without attacking it."
    </point>
    <point>
      If relationships were affected before, be careful not to let insecurity keep driving them. Persistent thoughts like "I'm still the unattractive version of me" can lead to reassurance-seeking, comparison, and pulling away. When you notice that pattern, name it directly instead of acting from it.
    </point>
    <point>
      Keep your motivation health-centered. If all your self-worth gets tied to appearance, the discomfort usually just shifts rather than disappears. Continue eating well and exercising because they support your health, stability, and functioning—not just because they change how you look.
    </point>
    <point>
      If this disconnect keeps feeling strong, talk to a therapist, especially one familiar with body image or self-esteem work. The issue you described is mental and emotional now, and it is reasonable to get help for that the same way you addressed the physical side.
    </point>
    <point>
      A practical exercise: write down three things each day that reflect your current reality, not your old identity. For example: "I followed my routine," "I feel stronger," "My body is different from a year ago." Repetition helps update the way you see yourself.
    </point>
    <point>
      Your target should not be "become fully confident immediately." Aim for a more accurate self-perception. Confidence usually grows after that.
    </point>
  </advice>

    </point>
    <point>
      Use objective anchors instead of relying on your mood in the mirror.     </point>

      Keep your motivation health-centered. If all your self-worth gets tied to appearance, the discomfort usually just shifts rather than disappears. Continue eating well and exercising because they support your health, stability, and functioning—not just because they change how you look.

      If this disconnect keeps feeling strong, talk to a therapist, especially one familiar with body image or self-esteem work. The issue you described is mental and emotional now, and it is reasonable to get help for that the same way you addressed the physical side.

    </point>
    <point>
      Your target should not be "become fully confident immediately." Aim for a more accurate self-perception. Confidence usually grows after that.
    </point>
  </advice>

response:
<advice>You should not end this right before you leave. Go on the trip, but only after having a direct conversation that is narrower and more accountable than the fights you’ve been having.</advice>
  <advice>What you need to say is closer to: “The security and follow-through issues are real, and I understand why they make you feel you can’t rely on me. I don’t want to keep debating whether your feelings are valid. I do want us to use therapy to figure out whether this can actually improve.”</advice>
  <advice>Do not use the trip as a “perfect time” to break up for her benefit. If you want to end the relationship, own that as your decision. If you do not want to end it now, then do not frame your leaving as a test of whether she should leave you.</advice>
  <advice>You also need to stop describing the issue as mainly her anger toward you. The more accurate version, based on your own post, is: you have a chronic reliability problem, especially around safety and mental load; she responds with accumulating resentment and anger; and the two of you then communicate in a way that makes repair fail.</advice>
  <advice>That means therapy has a real target. It is not supposed to stop all mistakes forever. It is supposed to help with at least four things:</advice>
  <advice>
    <point>how serious each type of lapse is, especially doors, security, and safety;</point>
    <point>what systems you will use so this is not just “I’ll try harder”;</point>
    <point>what accountability and repair should look like after a mistake;</point>
    <point>how she can express anger without storing every past injury and detonating over the current one.</point>
  </advice>
  <advice>You should treat the security issues as non-negotiable and create concrete safeguards before you leave. For example: a nightly door-lock checklist, alarms/reminders, a written closing routine for her office, and any physical systems that reduce reliance on memory alone. “I’m forgetful” is an explanation, not a sufficient plan.</advice>
  <advice>If you suspect ADHD, then address it seriously. That does not have to mean medication if you do not want medication, but it does mean evaluation, evidence-based coping strategies, and a willingness to be measured by outcomes. If the same safety failures keep happening, “I’m trying” will keep landing badly because from her side the impact is unchanged.</advice>
  <advice>During conflict, stop asking global questions like “Why do you stay?” or saying “It feels like you hate me.” Those statements escalate, invite reassurance, and shift focus away from the concrete issue. Replace them with specific repair language: “I see why this scared/angered you. Here is what I will change so this exact thing is less likely to happen again.”</advice>
  <advice>At the same time, therapy should not become a project where only you are the problem. Her pattern of never letting incidents resolve, stacking years of mistakes into every present conflict, and making it impossible for you to apologize, explain, or repair is also unsustainable. Even justified anger can become destructive if there is no path back from it.</advice>
  <advice>So the practical answer is: wait, go to therapy, and use the time before and during the trip to set up concrete systems and a better framework for discussing mistakes. Then judge the relationship by whether both of you can change the pattern, not by whether love exists. Love is already present; what is in doubt is whether the relationship can become safe, workable, and repairable.</advice>
  <advice>If after a period of therapy the same cycle remains—serious lapses from you, permanent resentment from her, no effective repair—then breaking up would be more honest than continuing a relationship where both of you feel trapped by love and hurt at the same time.</advice>

<response>
  <advice>You should not end this right before you leave. Go on the trip, but only after having a direct conversation that is narrower and more accountable than the fights you’ve been having.</advice>
  <advice>What you need to say is closer to: “The security and follow-through issues are real, and I understand why they make you feel you can’t rely on me. I don’t want to keep debating whether your feelings are valid. I do want us to use therapy to figure out whether this can actually improve.”</advice>
  <advice>Do not use the trip as a “perfect time” to break up for her benefit. If you want to end the relationship, own that as your decision. If you do not want to end it now, then do not frame your leaving as a test of whether she should leave you.</advice>
  <advice>You also need to stop describing the issue as mainly her anger toward you. The more accurate version, based on your own post, is: you have a chronic reliability problem, especially around safety and mental load; she responds with accumulating resentment and anger; and the two of you then communicate in a way that makes repair fail.</advice>
  <advice>That means therapy has a real target. It is not supposed to stop all mistakes forever. It is supposed to help with at least four things:</advice>
  <advice>
    <point>how serious each type of lapse is, especially doors, security, and safety;</point>
    <point>what systems you will use so this is not just “I’ll try harder”;</point>
    <point>what accountability and repair should look like after a mistake;</point>
    <point>how she can express anger without storing every past injury and detonating over the current one.</point>
  </advice>
  <advice>You should treat the security issues as non-negotiable and create concrete safeguards before you leave. For example: a nightly door-lock checklist, alarms/reminders, a written closing routine for her office, and any physical systems that reduce reliance on memory alone. “I’m forgetful” is an explanation, not a sufficient plan.</advice>
  <advice>If you suspect ADHD, then address it seriously. That does not have to mean medication if you do not want medication, but it does mean evaluation, evidence-based coping strategies, and a willingness to be measured by outcomes. If the same safety failures keep happening, “I’m trying” will keep landing badly because from her side the impact is unchanged.</advice>
  <advice>During conflict, stop asking global questions like “Why do you stay?” or saying “It feels like you hate me.” Those statements escalate, invite reassurance, and shift focus away from the concrete issue. Replace them with specific repair language: “I see why this scared/angered you. Here is what I will change so this exact thing is less likely to happen again.”</advice>
  <advice>At the same time, therapy should not become a project where only you are the problem. Her pattern of never letting incidents resolve, stacking years of mistakes into every present conflict, and making it impossible for you to apologize, explain, or repair is also unsustainable. Even justified anger can become destructive if there is no path back from it.</advice>
  <advice>So the practical answer is: wait, go to therapy, and use the time before and during the trip to set up concrete systems and a better framework for discussing mistakes. Then judge the relationship by whether both of you can change the pattern, not by whether love exists. Love is already present; what is in doubt is whether the relationship can become safe, workable, and repairable.</advice>
  <advice>If after a period of therapy the same cycle remains—serious lapses from you, permanent resentment from her, no effective repair—then breaking up would be more honest than continuing a relationship where both of you feel trapped by love and hurt at the same time.</advice>
</response>

response:
<advice>You should probably end it, or at minimum stop treating this as something that is on its way to a relationship.</advice>
  <advice>The key fact is not whether he is a bad person, whether work is truly busy, or whether your last conversation was phrased perfectly. The key fact is that he told you plainly that what he is giving is all he can give right now. Believe that.</advice>
  <advice>If what he can give right now leaves you feeling anxious, under-prioritized, and like you have to carry the connection, then this is not working for you. That does not mean either of you is wrong. It means the fit is wrong.</advice>
  <advice>Do not stay on the basis of chemistry, early intensity, or how special he made you feel at the beginning. A lot of people can feel amazing in the first few weeks. What matters more is the stable pattern that follows. The stable pattern here is: he pulled back, you pursued, and he confirmed he is not offering more.</advice>
  <advice>Also be careful not to let loneliness or wanting to get out of the house make this decision for you. If part of the appeal is escape, that will make it much harder to walk away from something that is emotionally unsatisfying. Try to separate “I miss him” from “I hate being home” and “I feel lonely.” Those are not the same problem.</advice>
  <advice>If you do continue, only do it if you can sincerely accept it as casual, limited, and unlikely to deepen soon. Not “I’ll stay and hope.” Not “maybe if I’m patient.” Only “this is enough for me as it is.” From what you wrote, it does not sound like it is enough for you.</advice>
  <advice>If you end it, keep it simple: tell him you like him, but you want a level of consistency and intention that he has said he cannot give right now, so you are stepping away. Do not argue the texting details again. The mismatch is already clear.</advice>
  <advice>A useful rule here: when someone says “this is all I can give,” your job is not to decode whether they might someday give more. Your job is to decide whether what they are giving now is enough for you.</advice>

<response>
  <advice>You should probably end it, or at minimum stop treating this as something that is on its way to a relationship.</advice>
  <advice>The key fact is not whether he is a bad person, whether work is truly busy, or whether your last conversation was phrased perfectly. The key fact is that he told you plainly that what he is giving is all he can give right now. Believe that.</advice>
  <advice>If what he can give right now leaves you feeling anxious, under-prioritized, and like you have to carry the connection, then this is not working for you. That does not mean either of you is wrong. It means the fit is wrong.</advice>
  <advice>Do not stay on the basis of chemistry, early intensity, or how special he made you feel at the beginning. A lot of people can feel amazing in the first few weeks. What matters more is the stable pattern that follows. The stable pattern here is: he pulled back, you pursued, and he confirmed he is not offering more.</advice>
  <advice>Also be careful not to let loneliness or wanting to get out of the house make this decision for you. If part of the appeal is escape, that will make it much harder to walk away from something that is emotionally unsatisfying. Try to separate “I miss him” from “I hate being home” and “I feel lonely.” Those are not the same problem.</advice>
  <advice>If you do continue, only do it if you can sincerely accept it as casual, limited, and unlikely to deepen soon. Not “I’ll stay and hope.” Not “maybe if I’m patient.” Only “this is enough for me as it is.” From what you wrote, it does not sound like it is enough for you.</advice>
  <advice>If you end it, keep it simple: tell him you like him, but you want a level of consistency and intention that he has said he cannot give right now, so you are stepping away. Do not argue the texting details again. The mismatch is already clear.</advice>
  <advice>A useful rule here: when someone says “this is all I can give,” your job is not to decode whether they might someday give more. Your job is to decide whether what they are giving now is enough for you.</advice>
</response>

response:
Don’t try to “tell them they’re being scammed” unless they ask. That wording, and even the attitude behind it, will probably make them dig in.

Instead, do three things:

<step>1. Stop using contemptuous language in your own head before you speak.</step>
If you go in thinking “they should have known better,” they will hear it. Replace that with: “They may be hopeful, under pressure, or not seeing the full picture yet.”

<step>2. Set boundaries without debating the business.</step>
You do not have to buy, host, promote, or join. Say it simply:
- “I’m not interested in MLM products, but I wish you well.”
- “I don’t do sales parties, so I’ll pass.”
- “Please leave me out of recruitment pitches.”

This protects you and avoids a fight.

<step>3. If you want to raise concern, ask questions instead of making declarations.</step>
Use neutral, practical questions that let them examine it themselves:
- “How much did you have to spend to get started?”
- “Have you worked out what you’d need to sell each month to profit?”
- “Are you required to keep buying inventory or materials?”
- “How much of the income comes from product sales versus recruiting?”
- “Have you tracked your hourly earnings so far?”

Those questions are much harder to dismiss than “this is a scam.”

If one of them seems doubtful or frustrated, that is the moment to be more direct—but still factual:
- “I’m concerned because a lot of these companies depend on sellers making very little after costs.”
- “If you want, I can help you look at the compensation plan and actual numbers.”

Focus on numbers, not judgment. Profit, expenses, time, pressure on friendships, and recruiting structure are all fair topics. “The products are tacky” is not useful.

Also, don’t make it a public argument on Facebook or in front of mutual friends. If you say anything, do it privately and briefly.

So the short version is:
- don’t insult them,
- don’t attack the product,
- don’t argue about whether they were foolish,
- do decline participation,
- and if invited into a real conversation, stick to calm questions and concrete financial reality.

That gives them the best chance to rethink it without feeling humiliated.

- (action: saying “two good friends of mine who I thought had a bit more sense than to sign up for multi-level marketing schemes”) That’s a pretty insulting way to frame your friends, and if that attitude comes through in person it would make the social circle feel judged rather than supported.
- (action: saying “The name is awful, the products look cheap, it’s expensive”) Dismissing something our friends are involved in that harshly can come off as contemptuous and make group conversations more tense.
- (plan: “I want to tell them that they’re wasting their time”) Even if well-meant, telling friends that directly could embarrass them and create conflict in the friend group.
SUPPORTS:
- (none)

<response>Don’t try to “tell them they’re being scammed” unless they ask. That wording, and even the attitude behind it, will probably make them dig in.

Instead, do three things:

<step>1. Stop using contemptuous language in your own head before you speak.</step>
If you go in thinking “they should have known better,” they will hear it. Replace that with: “They may be hopeful, under pressure, or not seeing the full picture yet.”

<step>2. Set boundaries without debating the business.</step>
You do not have to buy, host, promote, or join. Say it simply:
- “I’m not interested in MLM products, but I wish you well.”
- “I don’t do sales parties, so I’ll pass.”
- “Please leave me out of recruitment pitches.”

This protects you and avoids a fight.

<step>3. If you want to raise concern, ask questions instead of making declarations.</step>
Use neutral, practical questions that let them examine it themselves:
- “How much did you have to spend to get started?”
- “Have you worked out what you’d need to sell each month to profit?”
- “Are you required to keep buying inventory or materials?”
- “How much of the income comes from product sales versus recruiting?”
- “Have you tracked your hourly earnings so far?”

Those questions are much harder to dismiss than “this is a scam.”

If one of them seems doubtful or frustrated, that is the moment to be more direct—but still factual:
- “I’m concerned because a lot of these companies depend on sellers making very little after costs.”
- “If you want, I can help you look at the compensation plan and actual numbers.”

Focus on numbers, not judgment. Profit, expenses, time, pressure on friendships, and recruiting structure are all fair topics. “The products are tacky” is not useful.

Also, don’t make it a public argument on Facebook or in front of mutual friends. If you say anything, do it privately and briefly.

So the short version is:
- don’t insult them,
- don’t attack the product,
- don’t argue about whether they were foolish,
- do decline participation,
- and if invited into a real conversation, stick to calm questions and concrete financial reality.

That gives them the best chance to rethink it without feeling humiliated.</response>

response:
You need urgent in-person help, not just tips.

What you describe could be severe depression, dissociation, another psychiatric condition, a medical problem, substance-related effects, sleep-related problems, or some combination. The key point is this: going days without eating or drinking properly, losing track of time, eating rotten food, and thinking suicide may happen means this has crossed into a safety issue.

Do this next:

<step>1. If you might act on suicidal thoughts, or you feel unable to keep yourself safe today, call emergency services now or go to the nearest emergency department immediately.</step>
<step>2. If you are in the U.S. or Canada, call or text 988 now. If you are elsewhere, contact your local crisis line now. If calling feels hard, text if available.</step>
<step>3. Tell one real person today: “I am not safe being alone right now. I’ve been losing days, not eating, and I’m scared about suicide. I need you to stay with me or help me get urgent care.” Send that exact message to a parent, sibling, girlfriend, friend, resident advisor, or neighbor.</step>
<step>4. Get a medical/psychiatric assessment as soon as possible — ideally today or within 24 hours. If college counseling is unavailable, use a campus clinic, general doctor, urgent care, hospital, or public mental health service.</step>

What to say when you seek care:
“I’ve been losing track of days. I sometimes don’t eat, drink water, or bathe. I’ve eaten rotten food. I disappear and don’t remember what happened. I’m scared I may become suicidal if this continues.”

That wording will help them understand the urgency.

Until you are seen, focus only on safety, not self-improvement:

<immediate>
  <item>Do not stay completely isolated if you can avoid it. Be around another person, or have someone check on you regularly.</item>
  <item>Throw away all spoiled food.</item>
  <item>Drink water now.</item>
  <item>Eat something simple and safe now — bread, fruit, yogurt, rice, eggs, soup, anything easy.</item>
  <item>Do not use alcohol or drugs.</item>
  <item>Put distance between yourself and anything you could use to harm yourself if you are feeling at risk.</item>
  <item>Set alarms for every 2–3 hours labeled: water, food, bathroom, message someone.</item>
</immediate>

For the next 48 hours, use a bare-minimum checklist:
<checklist>
  <item>Drink water 4–6 times a day</item>
  <item>Eat 2 simple meals</item>
  <item>Shower or wash face and brush teeth</item>
  <item>Text one person back</item>
  <item>Leave your room once</item>
  <item>Attend or arrange urgent care</item>
</checklist>

Do not try to solve the “root cause” alone right now. Family history may matter, but memory gaps and this level of self-neglect need professional assessment first.

You should also warn your support people clearly, because they cannot help if they think you just flaked on plans. Send something short like:
“I’m sorry I disappeared. I’m dealing with serious mental health symptoms and periods where I lose track of time. I’m trying to get urgent help. If I go silent, please check on me.”

If you want, I can help you right now with one of these three things:
<option>A message to send to a parent/friend/girlfriend</option>
<option>A script to use when calling a clinic or crisis line</option>
<option>A 24-hour safety plan for tonight</option>
